skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: Painless postmenopausal vaginal spotting or bleeding of weeks to months duration. Quantify frequency, sanitary pad usage, colour, and whether blood is fresh red or dark brown.

skill.hx.obg.menstrual_history.expect: Exact age at natural menopause, years of amenorrhoea before the onset of bleeding, and character of previous menstrual cycles. Bleeding after menopause is never physiological.

skill.hx.obg.gynae_symptoms.expect: Watery or serosanguinous non-foul vaginal discharge, absence of severe pelvic pain in early disease, and presence of urinary frequency or tenesmus as markers of extrauterine spread.

chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history
chapters.blurb: Hyperoestrogenism, metabolic syndrome, tamoxifen use, and Lynch screening

skill.hx.obg.gynae_background.expect: Cervical screening history, prior pelvic ultrasound records, and absence of exogenous hormone replacement therapy or oral contraceptives.

skill.hx.endometria.risk.expect: Chronic unopposed oestrogen drive: obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, nulliparity, tamoxifen exposure, or family history of colorectal and uterine cancer indicating Lynch syndrome.

chapters.title: General physical examination
chapters.blurb: Nutritional status, pallor from chronic blood loss, and metabolic markers

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Obese central body habitus, conjunctival pallor from chronic blood loss, and absence of peripheral lymphadenopathy or cachexia in early disease.

skill.gen.vitals.expect: Blood pressure measurement to assess systemic hypertension as part of metabolic syndrome; hemodynamic stability and resting pulse rate.

chapters.title: Pelvic examination
chapters.blurb: Speculum visualisation of the cervix and bimanual uterine assessment

skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal.expect: Soft, non-tender obese abdomen without palpable suprapubic masses, hepatosplenomegaly, or ascites in early confined disease.

skill.exam.obg.speculum_inspect.expect: Atrophic vaginal mucosa and a smooth, healthy ectocervix with blood issuing from the external os, ruling out visible cervical cancer or prolapsing polyp.

skill.exam.obg.bimanual.expect: Mildly bulky, mobile, non-tender anteverted uterus with clear adnexa and soft, pliable parametria without sidewall fixity.

skill.endometrial.basics.title: Basics and pathophysiology of endometrial carcinoma
skill.endometrial.basics.oneLine: Dual Bokhman clinicopathological pathways, molecular classification, and mechanisms of local and nodal spread
skill.endometrial.basics.why: Understanding the biological distinction between oestrogen-dependent endometrioid tumours and aggressive non-endometrioid subtypes, together with modern molecular risk groups, informs surgical staging, prognostic risk, and adjuvant therapy selection.

teach.heading: Dual clinicopathological pathways: Bokhman classification
teach.body:
Endometrial cancer encompasses two distinct biological entities described by Bokhman.

Type 1 tumours (80-85 percent) are endometrioid adenocarcinomas arising from atypical endometrial hyperplasia under chronic unopposed oestrogenic stimulation. They are low-grade, oestrogen receptor-positive, typically diagnosed in postmenopausal women with obesity, and harbour PTEN, PIK3CA, and mismatch repair alterations.

teach.heading: Molecular subgroups and routes of neoplastic spread
teach.body:
The molecular classification defines four prognostic categories: POLE ultramutated (favourable prognosis), mismatch repair deficient (MMRd), no specific molecular profile (NSMP), and p53 abnormal (aggressive, poor outcome).

Spread occurs primarily through direct invasion through the myometrium to the serosa, transtubal dissemination into the peritoneal cavity, and lymphatic transport to pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes.

probes.q: What is the most common histological subtype of endometrial carcinoma, and what drives its progression from atypical hyperplasia?
probes.a: Endometrioid adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype, driven by prolonged unopposed oestrogenic stimulation.

probes.q: Which genetic alteration is classically present in over ninety percent of aggressive Type 2 uterine serous carcinomas?
probes.a: Mutations in the TP53 tumour suppressor gene resulting in abnormal p53 protein expression.

probes.q: Which molecular subgroup in modern classification carries an exceptionally favourable prognosis despite high histological grade?
probes.a: The POLE ultramutated subgroup, characterised by mutations in the exonuclease domain of DNA polymerase epsilon.

rubric.text: Contrasts Bokhman Type 1 endometrioid from Type 2 serous and clear cell carcinoma.
Explains the roles of PTEN, mismatch repair deficiency, and TP53 alterations.
Identifies the four molecular categories including POLEmut and p53 abnormal.

skill.endometrial.signs.title: Clinical features and physical examination findings in endometrial carcinoma
skill.endometrial.signs.oneLine: Recognising postmenopausal bleeding, evaluating pelvic examination findings, and identifying red flag signs
skill.endometrial.signs.why: Postmenopausal bleeding is the presenting symptom in over ninety percent of women with endometrial carcinoma. Correlating bleeding patterns with physical findings helps distinguish intrauterine neoplasia from lower genital tract lesions.

teach.heading: Cardinal presenting symptoms
teach.body:
Postmenopausal bleeding is the hallmark of endometrial carcinoma. Any bleeding occurring twelve months or more after the final menstrual period is postmenopausal bleeding and requires mandatory investigation.

Bleeding is typically painless, beginning as intermittent light spotting or pinkish discharge, which may become continuous or heavier over time. In perimenopausal women, presentation takes the form of heavy or irregular intermenstrual bleeding.

teach.heading: Physical examination findings and anatomical landmarks
teach.body:
General examination evaluates nutritional status, pallor from chronic blood loss, obesity, hypertension, and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.

Abdominal examination is usually unremarkable in early stages; a palpable hypogastric mass indicates advanced uterine enlargement, haematometra, or extrauterine pelvic extension. Flank fullness or shifting dullness suggests ascites from peritoneal dissemination.

teach.heading: Red flag signs and clinical pitfalls
teach.body:
Pyometra or haematometra may occur in elderly women when an intrauterine tumour obstructs a stenotic cervical os, presenting with lower abdominal ache and purulent discharge.

A dangerous pitfall is reassuring a patient because bleeding was small in volume or stopped spontaneously. The volume of bleeding does not correlate with stage or malignant invasion.

probes.q: What is the cardinal presenting symptom seen in more than ninety percent of patients with endometrial carcinoma?
probes.a: Postmenopausal bleeding, defined as any vaginal bleeding occurring one year or more after menopause.

probes.q: Why must speculum examination be performed carefully before concluding that bleeding originates from the uterine cavity?
probes.a: Speculum examination excludes bleeding lesions on the vulva, vagina, and cervix such as cervical carcinoma, polyps, or atrophy.

probes.q: What condition should be suspected when an elderly postmenopausal woman presents with pelvic cramp, foul purulent discharge, and a tender enlarged uterus?
probes.a: Pyometra secondary to cervical stenosis and obstructing endometrial malignancy.

rubric.text: Identifies postmenopausal bleeding as the primary presenting symptom requiring investigation.
Describes expected findings on speculum and bimanual examination in early versus advanced disease.
Recognises pyometra and cervical stenosis as potential presentations in elderly women.

skill.endometrial.summary.title: Synthesising the clinical picture in postmenopausal bleeding
skill.endometrial.summary.oneLine: Integrating bleeding duration, metabolic risk, physical examination, and ultrasound findings into a diagnostic synthesis
skill.endometrial.summary.why: Formulating a structured clinical summary allows the clinician to synthesise patient age, metabolic predisposition, bleeding chronology, and pelvic examination findings into a clear problem representation that justifies expedited tissue diagnosis.

teach.heading: Structuring the clinical synthesis
teach.body:
A rigorous clinical summary states four key elements: patient demographics and menopausal timeline, bleeding characteristics and volume, presence of hyperoestrogenic metabolic risk factors, and pelvic examination findings.

Framing the case as postmenopausal bleeding in a patient with risk factors establishes the pre-test probability and prevents diagnostic delay.

teach.heading: Synthesising initial triage and priority
teach.body:
Synthesising the presentation establishes an immediate priority: arranging transvaginal ultrasonography and outpatient endometrial biopsy without delay.

It communicates to the team that a normal cervical appearance in the presence of postmenopausal uterine bleeding points directly to an endometrial origin, requiring definitive histological sampling rather than empirical observation.

probes.q: What four key clinical dimensions must be combined in a summary of suspected endometrial carcinoma?
probes.a: Patient age and menopausal status, bleeding characteristics, metabolic risk factors, and pelvic examination findings.

probes.q: How does the presence of obesity, diabetes, and nulliparity influence the clinical synthesis in postmenopausal bleeding?
probes.a: It markedly raises the pre-test probability of oestrogen-driven Type 1 endometrioid adenocarcinoma.

probes.q: Why should normal speculum findings not delay referral in a woman presenting with postmenopausal bleeding?
probes.a: A healthy ectocervix confirms that bleeding originates from inside the uterine cavity, strengthening the indication for endometrial sampling.

rubric.text: Formulates a concise summary integrating bleeding story, metabolic profile, and examination.
Explains how risk factors increase suspicion of Type 1 endometrioid disease.
Identifies the necessity of immediate transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial biopsy.

skill.endometrial.differential.title: Differential diagnosis of postmenopausal and abnormal uterine bleeding
skill.endometrial.differential.oneLine: Distinguishing endometrial atrophy, polyps, hyperplasia, cervical carcinoma, and sarcomas from carcinoma
skill.endometrial.differential.why: Although postmenopausal bleeding is assumed malignant until proven otherwise, benign etiologies account for approximately ninety percent of presentations. Systematically evaluating atrophy, polyps, hyperplasia, and lower tract pathology prevents diagnostic errors while expediting oncology care.

teach.heading: Etiological landscape of postmenopausal bleeding
teach.body:
Endometrial atrophy accounts for 60 to 70 percent of postmenopausal bleeding, arising from mucosal friction and capillary fragility in an oestrogen-deficient environment.

Endometrial polyps cause 10 to 15 percent of cases, endometrial hyperplasia accounts for 5 to 10 percent, and endometrial carcinoma is diagnosed in approximately 10 percent. Cervical cancer, uterine sarcomas, and hormone-producing ovarian tumours constitute rarer but vital differentials.

teach.heading: Non-uterine and systemic causes
teach.body:
Extragenital bleeding sources must be actively distinguished from vaginal blood loss. Patients frequently confuse haematuria or rectal bleeding with vaginal bleeding.

Oestrogen-secreting ovarian sex cord-stromal tumours, such as granulosa cell tumours, can stimulate secondary endometrial proliferation and bleeding. Uterine sarcomas (leiomyosarcoma, endometrial stromal sarcoma) present with rapid uterine enlargement and abnormal bleeding.

probes.q: What is the single most common benign cause of postmenopausal vaginal bleeding?
probes.a: Endometrial atrophy or atrophic vaginitis secondary to hypoestrogenism.

probes.q: Which histological precursor lesion carries an approximate thirty percent risk of progression to invasive endometrioid adenocarcinoma if left untreated?
probes.a: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia, also termed endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN).

probes.q: Which ovarian sex cord-stromal neoplasm can produce postmenopausal bleeding by secreting excess oestrogen?
probes.a: Granulosa cell tumour of the ovary.

rubric.text: Lists the main causes of postmenopausal bleeding: atrophy, polyps, hyperplasia, and carcinoma.
Explains the progression risk of atypical hyperplasia / endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia.
Identifies non-uterine and extragenital sources including cervical and ovarian lesions.

skill.ix.endometrial.workup.title: Diagnostic evaluation, imaging and tissue sampling in suspected endometrial carcinoma
skill.ix.endometrial.workup.oneLine: Transvaginal ultrasonography, outpatient Pipelle suction curettage, pelvic MRI, and molecular MMR assessment
skill.ix.endometrial.workup.why: Transvaginal ultrasound serves as an initial non-invasive triage test, but histological confirmation via Pipelle sampling or hysteroscopic biopsy is required before surgery. Staging MRI and mismatch repair immunohistochemistry direct definitive surgical planning.

teach.heading: Transvaginal ultrasonography: triage threshold
teach.body:
Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is the first-line imaging triage test in postmenopausal bleeding.

An endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less in a postmenopausal woman has a high negative predictive value (greater than 99 percent for cancer).

A thin stripe does not exclude aggressive non-endometrioid tumours such as serous or clear cell carcinoma, so persistent or recurrent bleeding mandates histological sampling even when the thickness is 4 mm or less.

An endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm, or a focal mass, heterogeneous echotexture, or fluid collection, mandates histological tissue sampling.

rows: Useful if cervical stenosis prevents Pipelle

teach.heading: Staging imaging and pre-treatment workup
teach.body:
Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast is the gold standard imaging modality for pre-operative locoregional staging, assessing depth of myometrial invasion and cervical stromal infiltration.

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is indicated in high-grade tumours (serous, clear cell, G3 endometrioid) to detect nodal or distant peritoneal and pulmonary metastases. Serum CA-125 aids in monitoring advanced disease.

teach.heading: Mismatch repair testing and Lynch screening
teach.body:
Universal immunohistochemical screening for the four mismatch repair proteins (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) is recommended on all newly diagnosed endometrial carcinomas.

Loss of MSH2/MSH6 or isolated PMS2 strongly suggests Lynch syndrome. Loss of MLH1 is usually caused by somatic MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, tested via methylation analysis before genetic referral.

probes.q: What is the accepted endometrial thickness threshold on transvaginal ultrasound above which tissue sampling is indicated in postmenopausal bleeding?
probes.a: An endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm on transvaginal ultrasound requires histological sampling.

probes.q: Why is Pipelle suction curettage preferred over traditional operating theatre dilatation and curettage for initial sampling?
probes.a: Pipelle curettage is an outpatient procedure that avoids general anaesthesia, has lower cost, and causes less pain and perforation risk.

probes.q: Which imaging modality is superior for evaluating depth of myometrial invasion and cervical stromal involvement before surgery?
probes.a: Pelvic MRI with contrast.

rubric.text: Applies the 4 mm endometrial thickness threshold on transvaginal ultrasound.
Compares Pipelle suction biopsy with hysteroscopy and fractional curettage.
Explains the roles of pelvic MRI and universal mismatch repair immunohistochemistry.

skill.annex.endometrial.figo_molecular.title: FIGO staging and molecular classification of endometrial carcinoma
skill.annex.endometrial.figo_molecular.oneLine: Surgical FIGO staging system and integration of the four Proactive Molecular Risk Groups
skill.annex.endometrial.figo_molecular.why: Endometrial carcinoma is surgically staged. Integrating anatomical spread with molecular profiling (POLEmut, MMRd, NSMP, p53abn) provides an accurate framework that guides adjuvant radiotherapy and systemic treatment choices.

teach.heading: FIGO anatomical staging system
teach.body:
Staging of endometrial cancer is surgical and pathological, established following total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

Stage I is confined to the uterine corpus (IA: inner half of myometrium; IB: outer half of myometrium). Stage II invades cervical stroma. Stage III exhibits regional spread to serosa, adnexa, vagina, or lymph nodes. Stage IV invades bladder or bowel mucosa, or has distant metastases.

rows: Tumour limited to endometrium or < 50% myometrial invasion
Cervical stromal invasion without extrauterine spread
Bladder / bowel mucosa (IVA), distant / inguinal nodes (IVB)

teach.heading: The four molecular risk subgroups
teach.body:
The molecular classification refines prognosis beyond morphology:

1. POLE ultramutated (POLEmut): 5-10%, excellent prognosis, permits de-escalation of adjuvant therapy.
2. Mismatch repair deficient (MMRd): 25-30%, intermediate prognosis, eligible for immune checkpoint blockade.
3. No specific molecular profile (NSMP): 45-50%, intermediate prognosis, hormone receptor positive.
4. p53 abnormal (p53abn): 10-15%, aggressive, poor prognosis, requires systemic chemotherapy.

probes.q: What distinguishes FIGO Stage IA from Stage IB in endometrial carcinoma?
probes.a: Stage IA has less than 50 percent myometrial invasion, whereas Stage IB has 50 percent or more myometrial invasion.

probes.q: What anatomical involvement defines FIGO Stage II endometrial cancer?
probes.a: Tumour invasion into the cervical stroma without extension beyond the uterus.

probes.q: How does FIGO Stage IIIC1 differ from Stage IIIC2?
probes.a: Stage IIIC1 involves regional pelvic lymph nodes, whereas Stage IIIC2 involves para-aortic lymph nodes with or without pelvic nodes.

rubric.text: Outlines the anatomical criteria for FIGO Stages I through IV.
Differentiates Stage IA (< 50% myometrium) from Stage IB (>= 50% myometrium).
Summarises the four molecular subgroups: POLEmut, MMRd, NSMP, and p53abn.

skill.endometrial.diagnosis.title: Formulating the definitive diagnosis and risk stratification in endometrial carcinoma
skill.endometrial.diagnosis.oneLine: Integrating histological subtype, FIGO architectural grade, myometrial invasion depth, LVSI, and molecular groups
skill.endometrial.diagnosis.why: Final diagnosis and staging in endometrial carcinoma are pathological and surgical. Combining histological subtype, architectural grade, myometrial invasion depth, lymphovascular space invasion, and molecular markers assigns patients to risk categories that govern adjuvant therapy.

teach.heading: FIGO architectural grading of endometrioid carcinoma
teach.body:
Histological grading applies to endometrioid carcinomas and reflects the proportion of solid non-squamous tumour growth:

Grade 1: 5 percent or less solid non-squamous growth pattern (well-differentiated).
Grade 2: 6 to 50 percent solid non-squamous growth pattern (moderately differentiated).
Grade 3: greater than 50 percent solid non-squamous growth pattern (poorly differentiated). Severe nuclear atypia upgrades G1 or G2 by one grade.

rows: Stage IA, Grade 1-2 endometrioid, LVSI negative
Stage IA Grade 3, or Stage IB Grade 1-2
Stage IB Grade 3, or substantial LVSI
Stage II-III, serous / clear cell, p53 abnormal

teach.heading: Non-endometrioid and molecular integration
teach.body:
Non-endometrioid subtypes (serous carcinoma, clear cell carcinoma, carcinosarcoma) are all designated high-grade tumours by definition, regardless of architectural pattern.

Immunohistochemical staining for mismatch repair proteins (MMRd) and p53, together with POLE mutation analysis, completes the diagnostic formulation. A p53-abnormal tumour moves patients into high-risk protocols, while POLE mutation confirms a favourable course.

probes.q: What architectural criterion separates FIGO Grade 1 from Grade 2 endometrioid adenocarcinoma?
probes.a: Grade 1 has 5 percent or less solid non-squamous growth, whereas Grade 2 has 6 to 50 percent solid growth.

probes.q: Why are uterine serous carcinomas and clear cell carcinomas not assigned a numerical FIGO grade?
probes.a: They are high-grade tumours by definition and behave aggressively regardless of architectural pattern.

probes.q: Which pathological features place a patient with Stage I endometrioid cancer into the high-intermediate risk category?
probes.a: Deep myometrial invasion of 50 percent or more (Stage IB), high tumour grade (Grade 3), or substantial lymphovascular space invasion.

rubric.text: Applies FIGO architectural grading criteria (G1 <= 5%, G2 6-50%, G3 > 50%).
Recognises serous and clear cell carcinomas as inherently high-grade malignancies.
Classifies patients into low, intermediate, high-intermediate, and high-risk categories.

skill.tx.endometrial.title: Surgical staging, adjuvant therapies, and systemic management of endometrial carcinoma
skill.tx.endometrial.oneLine: Minimally invasive hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, sentinel node mapping, and risk-tailored adjuvant therapy
skill.tx.endometrial.why: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and surgical nodal evaluation provides primary curative treatment. Tailoring adjuvant radiation, chemotherapy, or hormonal therapy according to pathological and molecular risk prevents recurrence while minimising treatment-related morbidity.
skill.tx.endometrial.dosingNote: This module teaches management at the level of modality and principle. Specific agents, routes, combinations and schedules must be taken from your current national or institutional guideline and local protocols at the time of prescribing. CliniX does not prescribe.

teach.heading: Primary surgical staging
teach.body:
The cornerstone of management is total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH-BSO).

Minimally invasive surgery (laparoscopic or robotic) is the preferred surgical approach over open laparotomy. It achieves identical oncological outcomes with substantially lower blood loss, fewer wound infections, and shorter hospital stays, which is particularly beneficial in obese and diabetic women.

teach.heading: Lymph node staging and surgical options

rows: Excision of external, internal, obturator nodes
Dissection up to the renal vessels
Gross pelvic nodes or high-risk features

teach.heading: Adjuvant radiotherapy modalities
teach.body:
Adjuvant radiation is tailored to pathological risk:

Vaginal brachytherapy (VBT) is the standard adjuvant treatment for intermediate and high-intermediate risk disease confined to the uterus, offering excellent local vaginal vault control with minimal bowel or bladder toxicity. External beam radiation therapy (EBRT) to the pelvis is indicated for Stage II disease, positive margins, or extensive lymphovascular space invasion.

teach.heading: Systemic chemotherapy and targeted immunotherapy
teach.body:
Platinum-based combination chemotherapy (carboplatin plus paclitaxel for six cycles) is standard for Stage III or IV disease, high-risk histology (serous, clear cell, carcinosarcoma), and node-positive disease.

In advanced or recurrent mismatch repair deficient (MMRd) endometrial carcinomas, immune checkpoint inhibition (such as pembrolizumab) demonstrates substantial and durable antitumor response. Endocrine therapy (megestrol acetate, letrozole) serves as a palliative option in hormone receptor-positive low-grade recurrence.

teach.heading: Indian clinical context and public schemes
teach.body:
In India, surgical staging and radiotherapy for endometrial cancer are covered under the Ayushman Bharat PMJAY scheme and state health assurance programmes.

Primary care and district hospitals must maintain a low threshold for referring women with postmenopausal bleeding to tertiary Regional Cancer Centres (RCCs). Minimally invasive surgical facilities and high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy units have expanded across government medical colleges.

probes.q: What is the primary surgical operation performed for clinical Stage I endometrial carcinoma?
probes.a: Total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, preferably via a minimally invasive laparoscopic approach.

probes.q: Which adjuvant radiation modality provides vaginal vault control with minimal rectal and urinary toxicity in intermediate-risk disease?
probes.a: Vaginal vault brachytherapy (VBT).

probes.q: Which systemic chemotherapy regimen is the standard first-line choice for advanced or high-risk endometrial carcinoma?
probes.a: Carboplatin and paclitaxel combination chemotherapy.

rubric.text: Recommends minimally invasive total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy as primary therapy.
Selects adjuvant vaginal brachytherapy or external beam radiation based on pathological risk.
Identifies carboplatin plus paclitaxel chemotherapy and immunotherapy for advanced disease.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Obese postmenopausal female (BMI approximately 31 kg/m2), comfortable in bed, alert and oriented. Mild conjunctival pallor. No supraclavicular, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. No jaundice or clubbing.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Pulse 78 beats/min regular and good volume; BP 138/86 mmHg; respiratory rate 16 breaths/min; temperature 36.8 C; SpO2 98% on room air. Haemodynamically stable.

skill.gen.edema.finding: No peripheral pedal oedema of bilateral lower extremities; no calf tenderness or signs of deep vein thrombosis.

skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal.finding: Abdomen is soft, obese, and non-tender throughout. No palpable suprapubic or abdominal mass; no hepatosplenomegaly. No shifting dullness or fluid thrill (no clinical ascites). Both renal angles non-tender.

skill.exam.obg.vulval_inspect.finding: External genitalia show physiological postmenopausal atrophic changes. No vulval ulcers, leukoplakia, excoriations, or discrete masses. Introitus is healthy with no active bleeding pooling at the vulva.

skill.exam.obg.speculum_insert.finding: Bivalve Cusco speculum inserted gently with warm water lubrication; well tolerated without discomfort or resistance.

skill.exam.obg.speculum_inspect.finding: Vaginal walls show mild postmenopausal atrophy. Cervix is flush with vault and smooth; external os is closed with a scant trickle of serosanguinous, blood-stained fluid issuing from the endocervical canal. No exophytic cervical growth, polyp, ulceration, or contact friability on the ectocervix.

skill.exam.obg.bimanual.finding: Uterus is anteverted, mildly bulky (approximately 8-week gestational size), firm, regular in contour, mobile, and non-tender. Cervix moves freely without excitation tenderness. Bilateral fornices and adnexa are clear without palpable masses or tenderness. Bilateral parametria are soft and pliable without induration reaching the pelvic sidewall. Pouch of Douglas is free.

skill.approach.obg.pelvic_close.finding: Speculum withdrawn under direct vision; perineum wiped cleanly, sheet replaced, and patient assisted to sit upright and dress in complete privacy.

skill.endometrial.signs.finding: Painless postmenopausal bleeding with a clear ectocervix and bloody discharge issuing from the os, a mildly enlarged uterine corpus (8-week size), and clear adnexa in an obese diabetic patient, highly characteristic of early endometrial neoplasia.

fbc.label: Full blood count (FBC / CBC)
fbc.result: Haemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, haematocrit 33%, total leucocyte count 6,800/uL with normal differential, platelet count 240,000/uL; red cell indices show mild microcytosis (MCV 77 fL, MCH 25 pg).
fbc.note: Mild microcytic hypochromic anaemia. Spotting of this light volume over two months alone rarely explains new microcytosis, so coexistent nutritional iron deficiency is likely; check iron studies and diet history rather than attributing the anaemia solely to endometrial blood loss.

tvs_pelvis.label: Transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS)
tvs_pelvis.result: Uterus measures 8.2 x 5.1 x 4.4 cm. Endometrium is diffusely thickened, heterogeneous, and echogenic, measuring 14 mm in double-layer thickness (normal postmenopausal <= 4 mm), with an irregular endometrial-myometrial junction. Bilateral ovaries appear atrophic and normal; no adnexal cystic or solid mass; no pelvic free fluid.
tvs_pelvis.note: Endometrial thickness of 14 mm markedly exceeds the 4 mm postmenopausal triage cut-off, confirming the urgent indication for histological endometrial sampling.

endometrial_biopsy.label: Pipelle endometrial biopsy and histopathology
endometrial_biopsy.result: Multiple fragments of endometrioid adenocarcinoma, FIGO Grade 1 (well-differentiated, solid non-squamous architecture less than 5 percent). Crowded back-to-back glands with cribriforming and nuclear atypia. Immunohistochemistry: strong diffuse oestrogen and progesterone receptor positivity; intact nuclear expression of MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 (mismatch repair proficient / NSMP molecular group); wild-type p53 pattern.
endometrial_biopsy.note: Definitive tissue diagnosis confirming well-differentiated endometrioid adenocarcinoma, Grade 1, mismatch repair proficient.

mri_pelvis.label: Contrast-enhanced pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
mri_pelvis.result: Endometrial mass confined to the uterine cavity and inner myometrium, invading approximately 30% of the total myometrial wall thickness (< 50% myometrial invasion). Intact outer myometrial rim; no disruption of the uterine serosa. Normal cervical stroma with no tumour infiltration into the cervix. Bilateral parametria are clear. No enlarged pelvic or common iliac lymph nodes.
mri_pelvis.note: Imaging suggests tumour confined to the inner myometrium (< 50% invasion) with clear cervical stroma, consistent with provisional radiological Stage IA and supporting primary surgical curative intent; definitive FIGO staging is surgical and pathological.

chest_xray.label: Chest X-ray (PA view)
chest_xray.result: Normal lung parenchyma without focal infiltrates, nodular metastases, or consolidation. Normal cardiothoracic ratio. Costophrenic and cardiophrenic angles are sharp.
chest_xray.note: No radiological evidence of pulmonary parenchymal metastases or pleural effusion; suitable for pre-anaesthetic clearance.

renal_liver_panel.label: Renal function tests and serum electrolytes
renal_liver_panel.result: Serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, blood urea 22 mg/dL, serum sodium 139 mEq/L, serum potassium 4.2 mEq/L, fasting blood glucose 132 mg/dL, HbA1c 7.1%. Total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, ALT 24 U/L, AST 22 U/L, serum albumin 4.0 g/dL.
renal_liver_panel.note: Normal baseline renal and hepatic function with reasonably controlled type 2 diabetes, confirming suitability for elective surgical staging.

ecg.label: 12-lead Electrocardiogram (ECG)
ecg.result: Normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min, normal PR and QRS intervals, normal electrical axis, no ST segment elevation, depression, or T wave inversion.
ecg.note: Normal baseline cardiac tracing providing cardiovascular clearance for general anaesthesia.

ca125.label: Serum CA-125 biomarker
ca125.result: Serum CA-125 level is 18 U/mL (normal reference range < 35 U/mL).
ca125.note: Normal baseline CA-125, consistent with disease confined to the uterine corpus without overt peritoneal or nodal spread.

differentialModel.answer: Endometrial carcinoma. Primary differentials include endometrial hyperplasia with or without atypia, endometrial polyp, atrophic vaginitis or endometritis, carcinoma of the cervix, and submucosal fibroid uterus.

diagnosis.answer: Endometrial carcinoma with imaging suggesting disease confined to the inner half of the myometrium (provisional radiological Stage IA; definitive FIGO staging is surgical and pathological, assigned after total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy): well-differentiated endometrioid adenocarcinoma, Grade 1, presenting with postmenopausal bleeding in a patient with metabolic risk factors.

managementModel.answer: Refer to gynae-oncology multidisciplinary team for primary surgical staging with total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, sentinel lymph node mapping, and pathological risk stratification for adjuvant therapy.

total abdominal or laparoscopic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo oophorectomy
sentinel lymph node mapping or pelvic lymphadenectomy

risk stratification for adjuvant vaginal brachytherapy
counselling on diagnosis surgical risks and surveillance follow up

teachingPoints: Postmenopausal bleeding is never normal or physiological; any vaginal bleeding occurring twelve months or more after the final menstrual period mandates urgent investigation to exclude endometrial carcinoma.

Transvaginal ultrasound is the primary non-invasive imaging triage test; an endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm in a postmenopausal woman requires histological sampling via outpatient Pipelle biopsy or hysteroscopy. Persistent bleeding requires sampling even with a thin stripe, since a thin measurement does not exclude serous or clear cell tumours.

Primary treatment and definitive staging for endometrial cancer is surgical: total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and sentinel lymph node assessment, with adjuvant vaginal brachytherapy reserved for intermediate-risk features.
Obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, nulliparity, and late natural menopause constitute the classic hyperoestrogenic metabolic risk triad that drives Type 1 endometrioid adenocarcinoma.
